clue.text: They bowed to the old king

definitions.text: They bowed to the old king

parts.words: They bowed to the old king
parts.note: the nursery rhyme's merry old monarch Cole called for his musicians, who drew bows across strings for him rather than bowing as courtiers

explanation.surface: Courtiers bend low before an elderly monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowed' suggests bending at the waist in respect; here it means playing a bowed string instrument. Old King Cole is the merry old soul of an English nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme Old King Cole calls for his trio of violinists, who play to him with their bows.

clue.text: What Selima failed to get, being in the wrong environment

definitions.meaning: Selima is the cat in Gray's Ode who drowned trying to catch goldfish in a tub
uncomfortable and out of place in unfamiliar surroundings

explanation.surface: Someone missed out because they were in an unsuitable setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray's 'Ode on the Death of a Favourite Cat, Drowned in a Tub of Gold Fishes' tells how the cat Selima fell in reaching for the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray's cat never landed the goldfish from the tub, and the idiom describes someone ill at ease in strange surroundings.

clue.text: Doctor in bed, laid up end of army career?

indicators.note: in means the doctor's letters go inside the other word
laid up in a down clue means the word bed is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, an army doctor

explanation.surface: A doctor stuck in bed, sick, at the end of a soldier's service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid up' suggests being ill in bed; in a down clue it turns BED upwards to DEB, with MO placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Release from military service is called demobilisation, shortened in British slang.

clue.text: With which to catch a ten-footer

definitions.text: With which to catch a ten-footer

parts.words: With which to catch a ten-footer
parts.note: a ten-footer sounds like something huge, but here it is a decapod crustacean with ten legs, caught in a baited trap

explanation.surface: Asking what gear lands a monster three metres long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ten-footer' suggests something ten feet long; it is a creature with ten feet, a decapod.
explanation.definitionFit: A wicker or wire trap is lowered to the seabed to catch this ten-legged shellfish.

clue.text: Second income for one on boards ?

definitions.text: Second income for one on boards ?

parts.words: Second income for one on boards ?
parts.note: 'income' read as a coming-in: an actor on the stage boards walks on again later in the scene

explanation.surface: An actor seeks a second source of earnings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Income' looks like money; read as 'coming in', it is an actor's return to the stage, 'the boards'.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor's later walk-on is a return to the stage; in general the word means coming back in.

clue.text: By whom the girl's upset (Ariadne ?)

indicators.note: upset means the letters are knocked over into a new order

parts.note: Sue is a girl's name; with the possessive it gives Sue's

explanation.surface: Someone upset a young woman, perhaps Ariadne herself.
explanation.walkthrough: THE and SUES (Sue's) are rearranged. In Greek myth Theseus abandoned Ariadne on Naxos after she helped him out of the labyrinth, so the whole clue also describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian hero deserted the Cretan princess on Naxos after she guided him through the labyrinth.

clue.text: Spar chopped in pieces in grate

indicators.note: a spar chopped up has its letters broken and reassembled

explanation.surface: A wooden pole is cut up for burning in the fireplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grate' looks like a fireplace; it is the verb meaning to scrape harshly.
explanation.definitionFit: To grate is to rub with a rough file or scrape harshly, which is what a coarse file does.

clue.text: Periodical a London school aims to produce

definitions.meaning: the British weekly news magazine founded in 1843

definitions.text: a London school aims to produce
definitions.meaning: the London School of Economics trains students in that discipline

explanation.surface: A magazine that a London college hopes to turn out.
explanation.walkthrough: The London School of Economics is a London university college.
explanation.definitionFit: It names both the weekly news magazine and a specialist in money and markets, the LSE's typical graduate.

clue.text: One of the administrative circles, in Paris ?

definitions.text: One of the administrative circles, in Paris ?

parts.words: One of the administrative circles, in Paris ?
parts.note: the French word for the city's districts literally suggests a rounding, and the twenty districts spiral outward

explanation.surface: A civil servant moving in Parisian official circles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Administrative circles' suggests official society; Paris is split into twenty numbered districts arranged in a spiral, each with its own town hall.
explanation.definitionFit: Paris is divided into twenty municipal districts, and the French word for one comes from a verb meaning to make round.

clue.text: The note isn't half long!

parts.note: British 'isn't half' means 'is very', but literally the note is half of an old note value whose Latin name means short

explanation.surface: An exclamation that some musical note goes on and on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Isn't half long' is British slang for 'is really long'; the whole note is indeed the longest note in common use, and its name literally means half a breve.
explanation.definitionFit: This whole note is held for four beats, and its name means half of the old breve note value.

clue.text: River takes direction to the old town

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
taken as written
Ur is the ancient Sumerian city, the crossword's favourite old town

explanation.surface: A river picks a course towards an ancient settlement.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stour is the name of several English rivers, notably in Kent, Dorset and Suffolk.

clue.text: The way of the world for instance

definitions.text: The way of the world for instance

parts.words: The way of the world for instance
parts.note: read literally, the path a planet such as the Earth follows round the sun, not the idiom about how things go

explanation.surface: A remark that this is simply how life goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The way of the world' is an idiom for how things usually are; read literally it is the path our planet travels.
explanation.definitionFit: A planet's path around the sun is its circuit through space, so Earth's route is one example.

clue.text: One joining the row in the theatre

definitions.meaning: someone who ties things together, a binder or knotter
a raised bank of seats, as in a circle or gallery

explanation.surface: Someone takes their place in a line of seats at a play.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who ties things is a joiner of sorts, and a theatre's banked rows of seats are each one level.

clue.text: Bird's double act

indicators.note: double means the following word's letters appear twice in a row

parts.note: to do is to act

explanation.surface: A comedy duo performs as a pair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Double act' reads as a comedy pairing; instead it means 'act' taken twice.
explanation.definitionFit: The extinct flightless bird of Mauritius is the classic example of a vanished species.

clue.text: Way into church — no way one starts a race

parts.note: O is a nought, nothing
RD is the abbreviation for road
I is the Roman numeral for one
a nation is a people or race

explanation.surface: Entering the Church means not using the usual road at the start of a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts a race' suggests a sporting start; it just puts I before NATION.
explanation.definitionFit: Being formally made a priest or minister is how a person enters the clergy.

clue.text: Hatter's little bat resembled a heavenly cup-bearer

definitions.text: Hatter's little bat resembled a heavenly cup-bearer

parts.words: Hatter's little bat resembled a heavenly cup-bearer
parts.note: in Alice in Wonderland the Hatter sings 'Twinkle, twinkle, little bat' with the line comparing the bat to a serving board 'in the sky'

explanation.surface: The Mad Hatter's song likens a small bat to a celestial servant.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hatter's parody of 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' runs 'Up above the world you fly, like a tea-tray in the sky'. 'Cup-bearer' suggests Ganymede, but it is a board carrying cups.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat board for carrying cups and saucers is literally what bears cups, and the Hatter's song puts one in the sky.

clue.text: A lot of players, about exhausted, gave up

indicators.note: about means the band's letters go around the next word

parts.note: a band is a group of musicians
done in means worn out, so done is exhausted

explanation.surface: Worn-out players in a large troupe finally quit.
explanation.definitionFit: To abandon something is to quit or desert it entirely.

clue.text: No gaps in these ranks

parts.note: describes rows of soldiers pressed close together, the adjective usually paired with 'ranks'

explanation.surface: Soldiers stand shoulder to shoulder in tight formation.
explanation.walkthrough: The adjective is almost always met in the phrase 'serried ranks'; the clue describes it rather than defining with a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Packed tightly together with no space between, as soldiers standing shoulder to shoulder are.

clue.text: Fine meal includes a starter of vegetables in season

indicators.note: includes means the flour takes the next letters inside it

parts.note: flour is finely ground meal

indicators.note: a starter of means only the opening letter of vegetables is used

explanation.surface: A good dinner features a first course of vegetables that are currently in season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Season' looks like a time of year, but it is the verb meaning to add taste to food.
explanation.definitionFit: To season a dish is to give it taste with salt, herbs or spices.

clue.text: Composer reformed sins in a French king

indicators.note: in means the rearranged letters sit inside the king

parts.note: roi is French for king

indicators.note: reformed means the letters of sins are formed anew

explanation.surface: A musician repents his sins while in a French monarch's court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformed sins' suggests repentance; it is an anagram signal turning SINS into SSIN, inside ROI.
explanation.definitionFit: Gioachino Rossini wrote The Barber of Seville and William Tell, Italian operas.

clue.text: What can be made with a bare bodkin ?

definitions.text: What can be made with a bare bodkin ?

parts.words: What can be made with a bare bodkin ?
parts.note: quotes Hamlet's soliloquy, where a man might settle his own account and end life with a mere dagger

explanation.surface: A question about what a simple needle can make.
explanation.walkthrough: A bodkin looks like a sewing needle; in Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' it is a dagger: 'When he himself might his quietus make with a bare bodkin'.
explanation.definitionFit: It means release from life, death, or settlement of a debt; Hamlet imagines achieving it by suicide with a dagger.

clue.text: Found not guilty ? Bill thus left

indicators.note: thus links the courtroom verdict to the bill taken away, saying this is what remains

parts.note: acquitted means cleared of a charge in court
AC is short for account, a bill

explanation.surface: Cleared in court, a man has his bill paid and walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark shows the verdict word is to be cut: remove AC (account, a bill) from ACQUITTED and what is left means 'left'.
explanation.definitionFit: To have quit a place, in older usage, is to have departed or gone away from it.

clue.text: From the start of our era a return to opera

indicators.note: a return means the letters just gathered are read backwards

parts.note: the first year of the Christian era is AD 1, written AD I

explanation.surface: Since the beginning of the modern age, a comeback for grand opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return' turns ADIA (AD I, the first year of our era, plus A) backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's grand work set in ancient Egypt is one of the best-known pieces in the repertoire.

clue.text: Knock it back as the aperitif ?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: back means the word it is read in reverse order

explanation.surface: Down your drink in one, as befits a pre-dinner tipple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock it back' suggests downing a drink, but 'back' just turns IT round to TI, put after AS.
explanation.definitionFit: The sparkling Italian wine from Piedmont is a typical drink served before a meal; the question mark admits it is one example.

clue.text: One of 'three that stopped Atalanta

parts.note: in Greek myth Hippomenes dropped golden fruit during a footrace, and the runner paused to pick each one up

explanation.surface: A reference to the trio of objects that halted a famous runner.
explanation.walkthrough: Atalanta, the swift huntress of Greek myth, lost her race to Hippomenes because she stopped to collect three golden fruits he threw down.
explanation.definitionFit: The golden fruits given by Aphrodite were the orchard fruit of Eden fame, rolled aside to distract the racer.

clue.text: Academic republican ?

parts.note: the Greek philosopher founded the Academy in Athens and wrote the Republic

explanation.surface: Asking about a scholar with anti-monarchist politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Academic' and 'republican' look like a description of a politics professor; they point to the founder of the Academy and author of The Republic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian thinker founded the original Academy and wrote a dialogue on the ideal state, The Republic.

clue.text: No record will be set up by a labourer

indicators.note: set up in a down clue means the letters are raised, so read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A worker will never cut a single.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' turns the whole of NO + EP backwards in this down clue, giving the letters upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin America a peon is an unskilled farm worker or day hand.

clue.text: Sea eagle captures one little boy-has he your number too?

definitions.text: little boy-has he your number too

indicators.note: captures means the eagle's name holds the next letter inside it

parts.note: the erne is the white-tailed sea eagle
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A sea eagle seizes a small child, who may know your phone number.
explanation.walkthrough: The name is a diminutive boy's name, and also the Premium Bond machine that picks winning numbers in Britain; Premium Bonds are a UK savings lottery.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet form of Ernest suits a small boy, and the British Premium Bond prize computer shares the name, picking winners' numbers.

clue.text: Nice tart I get so involved with

indicators.note: the words get so tell us the fodder letters change into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to growing attached to a pleasant pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice tart' looks like a pastry, but NICE TART I is rearranged; 'with' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something complicated, with many tangled parts, is also called convoluted.

clue.text: Boone met his end in Montana, the dog

parts.note: Daniel Boone, the American frontiersman, shortened to Dan
met his end means died
taken as written
Mont is a standard abbreviation for the US state of Montana

explanation.surface: Frontiersman Boone died in Montana, and so did his dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The dog' at the end seems an afterthought; it is the definition, a terrier named after a character in Scott's Guy Mannering.
explanation.definitionFit: This small Scottish terrier breed takes its name from a farmer in a Walter Scott novel.
